clue.text: Labour PM – a dry and flipping slippery customer (6)

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the eel ends up facing the other way

blocks.note: TT = teetotal, and a teetotaller is dry
an eel is the proverbial slippery customer; flipped, it sits last

annotation.surface: A jibe at a Labour prime minister as a teetotal, untrustworthy operator.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Slippery customer' sounds like a verdict on the politician, but it is just the fish. 'Flipping' also passes as a mild British curse.
annotation.definitionFit: Clement Attlee led Britain's post-war Labour government from 1945 to 1951, so he is a Labour PM by name.

clue.text: Realistic person’s yearly meeting – in part, it’s reorganised (10)

indicators.note: 'in' says the meeting is placed inside the other letters
to reorganise is to put into a new order, so the letters of 'part, it's' are rearranged

blocks.note: AGM = annual general meeting; it sits after the first two letters
PART + ITS rearranged, split around the meeting

annotation.surface: A sensible person's view of the annual general meeting: parts of it get rearranged.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's after 'person' stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay. 'In part' looks like a phrase meaning 'partly', but 'in' is the container signal and 'part' is fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone who deals with things practically rather than by ideals is realistic.

clue.text: Maybe German’s regret about frank, entertaining article (8)

indicators.note: turning something about faces it the other way, so the regret is written backwards
a host entertaining a guest has them inside the house, so OPEN holds the article

blocks.note: to rue = to regret; turned about, it leads off
the indefinite article, placed inside OPEN before its N

annotation.surface: A German's regret about some frank talk that included an article.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' flags a definition by example. The 's after German is 'has', a link.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Germany is in Europe, so a German is one of many kinds of European, which 'maybe' admits.

clue.text: Berks maybe and Yankee following aristocrat (6)

indicators.note: something following comes after, so Y goes after the aristocrat

blocks.note: Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet

annotation.surface: Berkshire, an American and a nobleman: the makings of a country house party.
annotation.walkthrough: Berks is the abbreviation for Berkshire, an English county west of London. It is also British slang for idiots, which is the reading the surface invites.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Berkshire, shortened to Berks, is one of the counties of England.

clue.text: In the nude in musical nightclubs (8)

indicators.note: 'in' says one thing is placed inside another, so the nude word goes in the musical

blocks.note: Cats, the Lloyd Webber musical, split after CA

annotation.surface: Nudity in a stage musical set in nightclubs.
annotation.walkthrough: The first 'In' belongs to the phrase 'in the nude'; the second 'in' is the container signal. Cabaret is itself a famous musical, a nice echo.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a cabaret is a nightclub or restaurant that puts on entertainment while guests eat and drink.

clue.text: A French commander accepting one is more disruptive (8)

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so the commander takes in the one

blocks.note: I = one, the Roman numeral, placed inside RULER

annotation.surface: A French officer taking someone on who turns out to be a troublemaker.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A French' is a translation: the French for 'a'.
annotation.definitionFit: A comparative synonym: unruly people disrupt order, and the -ier ending matches 'more'.

clue.text: President claiming one has hollow victories (8)

indicators.note: to claim something is to take hold of it, so TRUMP takes in the one
a hollow thing has nothing in the middle, so 'has' keeps only its outside letters

blocks.note: I = one, placed inside TRUMP after TR

annotation.surface: A jibe that a president's claimed victories ring hollow.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the victories are hollow, but 'hollow' only empties 'has'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a triumph is a victory, especially a great or celebrated one.

clue.text: Ring friend, filled with energy (4)

indicators.note: something filled with a thing has it inside, so the friend holds the energy

annotation.surface: Phoning a friend while full of beans.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ring' reads as a phone call, but it is the sound of bells.
annotation.definitionFit: A noun sense: a peal is a loud ring of bells, so the verb-looking 'Ring' is a noun here.

clue.text: Drunkards call for help – about time! (4)

indicators.note: 'about' can mean around, so the call for help goes around the time

annotation.surface: Drunks shouting for help, and not before time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About time!' reads as an exclamation of impatience, but 'about' is the container signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: sot is an old word for someone habitually drunk.

clue.text: Rob Roy’s head stuck in brass instrument (6)

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
something stuck in a thing is lodged inside it, so the R goes inside the instrument

blocks.note: a bugle is a brass instrument
first letter of Roy, lodged after BU

annotation.surface: Rob Roy, the Scottish outlaw, with his head jammed in a bugle.
annotation.walkthrough: Rob Roy looks like one name, the Scottish folk hero, but the clue splits it: 'Rob' is the definition, a verb, and 'Roy' is the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with a twist: to burgle is to rob a building by breaking in.

clue.text: Italian lady expelling son, not heartless or uneducated (8)

indicators.note: to expel is to throw out, so the lady throws out the S
a heartless word has lost its centre, so NOT drops its O

blocks.note: SIGNORA, Italian for a lady, without S for son

annotation.surface: An Italian woman banishes her son, who is neither soulless nor unschooled.
annotation.walkthrough: S for son is a standard abbreviation, from family trees. 'Or' is a link, and 'not heartless' reads as a character reference.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: ignorant means lacking knowledge or schooling.

clue.text: Princess put on hair curlers and a kind of shoe (6,5)

indicators.note: in an across clue, a piece put on another is added to its end

annotation.surface: A princess getting ready: hair in curlers and choosing shoes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put on' suggests dressing up, which fits the princess, but it only tells you where the princess goes. The wordplay's split falls one letter away from the answer's word break.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose description: a roller skate is a boot or shoe fitted with wheels, so 'a kind of shoe' stretches only slightly.

clue.text: Doubts working cop in US is following lead for shooting (10)

indicators.note: something working is in operation, not in its original state, so the letters are rearranged
something following comes after, so the rearranged letters come after the S
the lead of a word is the letter that goes first

annotation.surface: Doubts about an American police officer who shoots first.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Is following' reads as one verb phrase, but 'is' is fodder and 'following' alone places the rearranged letters after S.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: suspicions and doubts are both feelings that something may not be true.

clue.text: Bloke is dancing around on small stone pillars (8)

indicators.note: dancing around moves the letters about, so they end up in a new order
in a down clue, a piece on another sits above it

blocks.note: S = small, as in clothing sizes

annotation.surface: A man dancing round some small standing stones.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Small stone' looks like a pebble, but 'small' is S and the definition starts at 'stone'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an obelisk is a tall, four-sided tapering stone pillar, like Cleopatra's Needle.

clue.text: Critical over committee’s computer equipment (8)

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece over another sits above it

blocks.note: a board is a governing committee

annotation.surface: A committee complaining critically about its IT kit.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's after committee is 'has', a link. 'Critical over' reads as 'angry about', but 'over' only stacks one piece on the other.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a keyboard is the hardware you type on, one piece of computer equipment.

clue.text: It holds hot liquids mother’s brewed (7)

indicators.note: brewing mixes ingredients together, so the letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters, including the S of 's

annotation.surface: A flask holding the tea that mother has made.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is ignored: 'mother's' supplies all seven letters. Brewing and hot liquids make the flask fit the scene neatly.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a Thermos is a vacuum flask, a container that keeps drinks hot.

clue.text: Former PM, one gutless Tory for the greater part (8)

indicators.note: a gutless word has had its insides removed, keeping just the outside letters

annotation.surface: A former prime minister dismissed as a spineless Conservative.
annotation.walkthrough: Tory is the nickname for a member of Britain's Conservative Party, which Major led.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: more than half of any group is its majority, the larger share.

clue.text: One glib criminal lacking honour (7)

indicators.note: criminal means bent or crooked, so the letters are twisted out of their order

annotation.surface: A smooth-talking crook with no sense of honour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' sits between fodder and definition, reading as a noun, but it is an adjective working on the words before it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: noble means honourable, and the ig- prefix negates it.

clue.text: Tuchel in job that’s changed? Me too! (4,3,4)

indicators.note: letters that have changed are no longer in their original order

annotation.surface: Thomas Tuchel, the German coach of the England football team, has changed jobs, and someone says they have too.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Join the club!' is said to someone sharing your bad luck. It also fits the surface: a football manager does join a club.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'join the club' tells someone you are in the same situation, which is what 'Me too!' says.

clue.text: Curry accompaniment served up, eating the French cake (6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' means read from the bottom, so the rice is written backwards
something eating another takes it inside, so the rice holds LA

blocks.note: rice is served with curry; turned up, it splits around LA

annotation.surface: Dessert time at a curry house, with a French pastry on the side.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Curry accompaniment' could be raita or naan, but only one side dish reads backwards as the shell of a French pastry.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: an eclair is a long cream-filled choux pastry, one kind of cake.

clue.text: Plans written up in annoying emails (4)

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' means read from the bottom, so the word is written backwards

blocks.note: maps = plans, as of a town or building

annotation.surface: Plans written up and sent out as unwanted emails.
annotation.walkthrough: MAPS read bottom to top gives SPAM. 'Written up' sounds like drafting a report, which suits the emails.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: spam is unwanted junk email, which is certainly annoying.

clue.text: Run round entering trendy club (4)

indicators.note: something entering a place goes inside it, so R and O go inside IN

annotation.surface: Someone rushing into a fashionable nightclub.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Club' reads as a nightclub, but it is a golf club. 'Round' looks like part of 'run round', but it is a separate piece.
annotation.definitionFit: A category member: an iron is a golf club with a flat metal head.

clue.text: Painting funny op art – it’s about right (8)

indicators.note: funny can mean odd or peculiar, so the letters are put out of order
'about' can mean around, so the assembled letters go around the R

blocks.note: R = right; it goes inside after the first two letters

annotation.surface: A comment on a playful piece of op art: it's pretty much correct.
annotation.walkthrough: Op art is abstract art built on optical illusions. 'It's about right' reads as approval, but the 's is 'is' and 'about' wraps the rearranged letters plus IT around R.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a portrait is a painting of a person, one kind of painting.

clue.text: How unfortunate! King meets head of Asian state (6)

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

annotation.surface: A sad tale of a king meeting an Asian head of state.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Head of Asian state' reads as a leader, but 'head of Asian' is just one letter and 'state' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Alaska is the largest of the fifty US states, bought from Russia in 1867.

clue.text: Day Blair follows old, dull routine (8)

indicators.note: something that follows comes after, so Blair comes after 'old'

annotation.surface: A day when Tony Blair trots out the same old tired routine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old, dull' reads as one description of the routine, but 'old' is wordplay and the definition starts at 'dull'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: monotony is tedious sameness, what a dull routine has.

clue.text: Partisan’s offer to capture area Sudanese vacated (6)

indicators.note: to capture something is to take it in, so the offer holds the other letters
a vacated place has been emptied, so Sudanese keeps only its outside letters

blocks.note: SUDANESE emptied to its outer letters

annotation.surface: A guerrilla fighter's offer to seize a region the Sudanese have abandoned.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Partisan' suggests a resistance fighter, but here it is an adjective: one-sided. The 's is 'has', a link.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a partisan view favours one side, which is what biased means.
